# 2 Maccabees Chapter 4 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 4 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_004_page_001.jpg

---

## Preamble

Chapter 4 charts the catastrophic corruption of the Jerusalem high priesthood under Seleucid pressure. Jason buys the office from Antiochus IV Epiphanes, introduces Hellenistic institutions including a gymnasium, and sets in motion a process of social collapse. His successor Menelaus is worse still — a murderer who engineers the assassination of the legitimate high priest Onias III. The three agents agree on structure but differ significantly on register, particularly in the gymnasium passages and the killing of Onias.

---

**1** The Simon mentioned above, who had informed about the money and about his own country, slandered Onias as if it were he who had incited Heliodorus and had been behind all the trouble.

**2** He dared to call this benefactor of the city, protector of his fellow citizens, and zealot for the laws an enemy of the state.

**3** But when his hostility went so far that murders were being committed by some of Simon's associates,

**4** Onias recognized the danger of the rivalry, and that Apollonius son of Menestheus and governor of Coelesyria and Phoenicia was intensifying Simon's malice.

**5** So he betook himself to the king — not to be an accuser of his fellow citizens, but with a view to the general and individual welfare of all the people.

**6** For he saw that without the king's attention it would be impossible to achieve peace in public affairs, or for Simon to stop his madness.

**7** But when Seleucus died and Antiochus, who was called Epiphanes, succeeded to the kingdom, Jason the brother of Onias obtained the high priesthood by corrupt means,

**8** promising the king three hundred and sixty talents of silver and eighty talents from another source of revenue.

**9** Beyond this he promised to pay a hundred and fifty more if authority were given him to establish a gymnasium and a corps of young men, and to enroll the people of Jerusalem as Antiochene citizens.

**10** When the king consented and Jason came to power, he immediately shifted his compatriots to the Greek way of life.

**11** Setting aside the royal privileges that had been secured for the Jews through John the father of Eupolemus — who had gone on the mission to establish friendship and alliance with the Romans — he abolished the lawful ways of living and introduced customs contrary to the law.

**12** With obvious enthusiasm he established a gymnasium right under the citadel, and he induced the noblest of the young men to wear the broad-brimmed Greek hat.

**13** There was such an extreme of Hellenization and adoption of foreign ways because of the surpassing wickedness of Jason, who was godless and no true high priest,

**14** that the priests were no longer zealous for the service of the altar. Despising the sanctuary and neglecting the sacrifices, they hurried to take part in the unlawful activities in the wrestling arena at the first call of the discus,

**15** thinking nothing of what their ancestors had honored, and regarding the Greek forms of prestige as the highest good.

**16** For this reason a heavy disaster came upon them, and the very men whose customs they had so eagerly sought to imitate became their enemies and punished them.

**17** For it is no light thing to act with impiety toward the divine laws — and the time that follows will make this plain.

**18** When the quinquennial games were being held at Tyre and the king was present,

**19** the vile Jason sent envoys as spectators, bearing three hundred silver drachmas as a contribution toward the sacrifice to Hercules. But the bearers themselves judged it improper to use the money for a sacrifice and considered it unsuitable for that purpose.

**20** So the sum intended by the sender for the sacrifice to Hercules was, by the decision of the bearers, redirected to the construction of triremes.

**21** When Apollonius son of Menestheus was sent to Egypt for the coronation of King Philometor, Antiochus learned that Philometor had become hostile to his government, and he took thought for his own interests. He went to Joppa and then proceeded to Jerusalem.

**22** He was received magnificently by Jason and the city, being welcomed with torchlight processions and acclamations, and afterward he led his forces into Phoenicia.

**23** After three years Jason sent Menelaus — the brother of the Simon mentioned above — to bring the money to the king and to settle certain urgent matters.

**24** But when Menelaus was presented to the king and appeared before him as a man of dignified bearing, he diverted the high priesthood to himself, outbidding Jason by three hundred talents of silver.

**25** He came back with the royal commission, bringing nothing worthy of the high priesthood. He had the disposition of a cruel tyrant and the rage of a savage beast.

**26** So Jason, who had ousted his own brother, was now ousted by another and driven as a fugitive into the territory of the Ammonites.

**27** Menelaus held the office but paid nothing of what he had promised to the king,

**28** in spite of repeated demands from Sostratus, the commander of the citadel — who was responsible for collecting the revenues. For this reason both men were summoned before the king.

**29** Menelaus left his brother Lysimachus as his deputy in the high priesthood; Sostratus left Crates, the commander of the Cyprian troops.

**30** While this was the state of affairs, the people of Tarsus and Mallus revolted because their cities had been given as a present to Antiochis, the king's concubine.

**31** So the king went in haste to settle the trouble, leaving Andronicus, a man of high rank, as his viceroy.

**32** Menelaus, thinking he had found a suitable opportunity, presented to Andronicus some of the gold vessels from the temple — pieces he had already been selling to Tyre and the surrounding cities.

**33** When Onias learned of this, he rebuked him openly, having first withdrawn for safety to the sanctuary at Daphne near Antioch.

**34** Therefore Menelaus, taking Andronicus aside, urged him to kill Onias. He went to Onias and, giving false assurances and pledging with an oath while extending his right hand, persuaded him — despite Onias's suspicions — to come out from the sanctuary. Without any regard for justice, he immediately had him killed.

**35** At this, not only the Jews but many from other nations were outraged and deeply grieved at the unjust murder of this man.

**36** When the king returned from the region of Cilicia, the Jews in the city, along with the Greeks who shared their indignation, appealed to him. They were grieved that Onias had been killed without any cause.

**37** Antiochus was genuinely grieved and moved to compassion. He wept because of the sobriety and uprightness of the deceased.

**38** Inflamed with anger, he immediately stripped Andronicus of his purple robe, tore off his outer garments, and led him through the whole city to the very spot where he had committed the outrage against Onias. There he put the murderer to death. The LORD repaid him with the punishment he deserved.

**39** When many acts of sacrilege had been committed throughout the city by Lysimachus with the connivance of Menelaus, and word of this spread abroad, the people gathered in force against Lysimachus — for large numbers of gold vessels had already been dispersed.

**40** As the crowds rose in revolt, filled with anger, Lysimachus armed about three thousand men and launched a violent, unjust attack, with a certain Auranus as leader — a man as advanced in age as he was in foolishness.

**41** When they realized what was happening, some seized stones, others blocks of wood, others scooped up handfuls of ash that lay nearby, and they hurled everything at Lysimachus and his men in wild confusion.

**42** They wounded many, killed some, and put all the rest to flight. The temple robber himself they killed next to the treasury.

**43** Charges were then brought against Menelaus in connection with the whole affair.

**44** When the king came to Tyre, three men sent by the council of elders laid the case before him.

**45** But Menelaus, already virtually convicted, promised a large sum of money to Ptolemy son of Dorymenes to win the king over.

**46** Ptolemy therefore drew the king aside into a colonnade, as if for refreshment, and induced him to change his mind.

**47** Menelaus — the cause of all the evil — he acquitted of all charges, while those unfortunate men who would have been freed even before a Scythian court he condemned to death.

**48** So those who had spoken up for the city and the villages and the sacred vessels suffered unjust punishment swiftly.

**49** Even the Tyrians were so outraged at the crime that they provided generously for the men's burial.

**50** As for Menelaus, he remained in office through the greed of those in power, growing worse in wickedness, and proving to be the chief schemer against his own fellow citizens.

---

## Translator's Notes

- **v. 9, "Antiochene citizens"**: Jason's request to register Jerusalemites as *Antiocheis* — citizens of Antioch — was an extraordinary step. It linked Jerusalem's elite to the Seleucid capital and subjected them to Greek civic norms.
- **v. 12, the gymnasium**: The gymnasium was far more than a sports facility — it was the central institution of Greek cultural formation, including Greek athletic training (which involved nudity), religious rites, and civic identity. Its placement "under the citadel" made the cultural challenge to the temple explicit.
- **v. 12, "broad-brimmed hat"**: The *petasos* — the hat of Hermes/Mercury. Wearing it was a visible marker of adopting Greek identity.
- **v. 19, the Hercules contribution**: The episode is revealing — even those committed to Jason's Hellenizing program drew the line at direct pagan sacrifice. The money was rerouted to shipbuilding.
- **v. 34, the murder of Onias**: Onias III is regarded as the last legitimate high priest in the Zadokite line. His murder by treachery — decoyed out of asylum under sworn oath — is treated by the author as a pivotal moral atrocity, sealing Menelaus's wickedness.
- **v. 47, "Scythians"**: Proverbially the most lawless of peoples. The comparison inverts: these men could have been acquitted before the most barbarous tribunal, yet Menelaus had them condemned before the king.
